topic_frame.original_topic: 디지털 치료제의 우울증 증상 완화 효과와 지속성
topic_frame.topic_en: The effectiveness and durability of digital therapeutics in alleviating depressive symptoms

independent: digital therapeutics (software-based therapeutic interventions for depression)
dependent: persistence/durability of symptom improvement over time
variables.population: individuals with depression or depressive symptoms
variables.context: digital health interventions for mental health treatment, including short-term effects and post-treatment follow-up

topic_frame.research_question: How effective are digital therapeutics at reducing depressive symptoms, and how long do these improvements persist after treatment?

sub_rqs.question: How effective are digital therapeutics at reducing depressive symptom severity in the short term compared with control conditions?
sub_rqs.rationale: Establishes the core post-treatment efficacy evidence base on which durability questions depend.
queries: digital therapeutics depression randomized controlled trial efficacy
internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy depressive symptoms meta-analysis
smartphone app intervention depression symptom reduction
prescription digital therapeutic major depressive disorder

sub_rqs.question: How long do reductions in depressive symptoms persist after digital intervention ends, based on follow-up assessments?
sub_rqs.rationale: Directly addresses the durability dimension of the topic through long-term follow-up evidence.
queries: digital intervention depression long-term follow-up sustained effect
internet CBT depression durability of treatment effects
digital mental health depression 12-month follow-up outcomes
relapse after computerized CBT depression
individual participant data network meta-analysis guided unguided internet CBT depression follow-up
internet-based CBT depression pooled effect size 6 to 12 month follow-up
long-term outcomes randomized trial online cognitive behavioural therapy depression 2-year follow-up

sub_rqs.question: How do effects and durability differ by intervention type, delivery format, and level of human support (guided vs. unguided)?
sub_rqs.rationale: Identifies design features of digital therapeutics that moderate effect size and persistence.
queries: guided versus unguided internet intervention depression effect
therapist support digital mental health intervention depression outcomes
app-based versus web-based depression intervention comparison
computerized CBT human support moderator effectiveness

sub_rqs.question: How do patient characteristics and clinical context (severity, comorbidity, primary care vs. community, adjunct vs. standalone use) moderate outcomes?
sub_rqs.rationale: Clarifies for whom and under which conditions digital therapeutics work and sustain benefit.
queries: moderators of digital intervention outcomes depression baseline severity
digital therapeutics adjunct to antidepressant treatment depression
eHealth intervention depression primary care effectiveness
digital CBT comorbid anxiety depression subgroup analysis
individual participant data meta-analysis baseline severity moderator internet depression treatment
meta-regression clinical setting comorbidity digital CBT depression effect size
blended or adjunctive digital CBT versus standalone depression randomized trial

sub_rqs.question: How do engagement, adherence, and attrition relate to symptom improvement and its persistence?
sub_rqs.rationale: Engagement is a key mechanism and threat to real-world effectiveness and durability.
queries: adherence engagement digital depression intervention symptom improvement
dropout attrition internet-delivered depression treatment
dose-response app usage depressive symptoms
machine learning predict engagement mental health app

sub_rqs.question: What methodological limitations, placebo or attention-control effects, and adverse effects affect the interpretation of digital therapeutic evidence for depression?
sub_rqs.rationale: Assesses evidence quality and risks, tempering conclusions about effectiveness and durability.
queries: risk of bias digital mental health depression trials
placebo sham control digital therapeutic depression
negative effects deterioration internet interventions depression
real-world effectiveness digital mental health depression

plan.search_strategy: Search 2010 to present, emphasizing systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and randomized controlled trials with adult or adolescent participants with depression or elevated depressive symptoms, plus regulatory-cleared prescription digital therapeutics studies. Exclude protocol-only papers, general wellness or prevention-only apps without depressive symptom outcomes, and non-digital telehealth that is purely video therapy. Expect rq2 (durability beyond 12 months) and rq6 (adverse effects and sham-controlled designs) to be the thinnest in the literature.

items.method: systematic review and network meta-analysis of double-blind RCTs
items.finding: Compares and ranks 21 antidepressant drugs for acute treatment of adult major depressive disorder. It does not evaluate digital interventions, though it offers a pharmacological benchmark.
items.limitations: Pharmacotherapy only, not digital therapeutics; abstract truncated before results.

items.method: meta-analysis of 12 RCTs
items.sample: 13 contrast groups, 2334 participants
items.finding: Internet-based CBT showed a small mean effect on depressive symptoms (FEA d=0.27, MEA d=0.32) with significant heterogeneity, reduced after removing an outlier study. Anxiety effects were large (d=0.96).
items.limitations: Early (2006) and small set of trials; heterogeneity and an outlier study; mixed depression and anxiety outcomes.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies comparing guided ICBT with face-to-face CBT
items.sample: 13 studies, N=1053 (2 on depressive symptoms)
items.finding: Guided ICBT and face-to-face CBT produced equivalent post-treatment effects overall (Hedges' g=-0.01, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.12). Study quality did not affect outcomes.
items.limitations: Only two studies on depression; few studies per condition; mixed psychiatric and somatic disorders; compares to active in-person treatment rather than control.

items.method: systematic review and individual patient data network meta-analysis of RCTs
items.sample: IPD from eligible RCTs of guided and unguided iCBT for depression (42 eligible studies per abstract)
items.finding: Estimates personalized short-term and long-term (6 and 12 month) relative efficacy of guided versus unguided iCBT for depression using PHQ-9 and patient characteristics. The abstract excerpt does not give the numerical results.
items.limitations: Abstract truncated before results; IPD available only from a subset of studies.

items.method: meta-analysis of 66 RCTs
items.sample: 66 RCTs of app-supported smartphone interventions (54 for depression)
items.finding: Smartphone interventions outperformed control conditions for depressive symptoms (g=0.28, n=54) and most effects remained robust after adjusting for control type and risk of bias. Effects were nonsignificant for some outcomes such as panic symptoms.
items.limitations: Transdiagnostic mental health scope; follow-up durability not shown in the excerpt.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 RCTs
items.sample: 9 RCTs, 1837 participants
items.finding: Smartphone psychological interventions reduced anxiety symptoms more than controls (g=0.325, 95% CI 0.17-0.48). It does not address depression.
items.limitations: Anxiety outcomes only; small number of trials.

items.method: individual participant data meta-analysis of RCTs
items.sample: 3876 participants from 13 of 16 eligible studies
items.finding: Pooled IPD from RCTs comparing self-guided iCBT with controls (usual care, waiting list, attention control) in adults with depressive symptoms, examining treatment outcome, response, and moderators. Specific effect sizes are not in the abstract excerpt.
items.limitations: IPD from only 13 of 16 eligible studies; missing data handled by imputation; abstract truncated.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 75 prospective studies
items.sample: 75 prospective articles
items.finding: Reviews prospective biomarkers (neuroimaging, immunology, hormones, etc.) predicting MDD onset and relapse. It does not address digital therapeutics.
items.limitations: Off-topic; biomarker prediction rather than treatment.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 RCTs
items.sample: 15 randomized trials of internet CBT for insomnia
items.finding: Evaluates internet-delivered CBT for insomnia on sleep efficiency and insomnia severity. Depression outcomes are not reported in the abstract.
items.limitations: Insomnia outcomes, not depression; abstract truncated.

items.method: narrative comprehensive review
items.finding: Reviews epidemiology, mechanisms and management of comorbidity between MDD and physical diseases. It offers context on comorbidity but no digital therapeutic evidence.
items.limitations: Narrative review without stated method; no digital intervention data.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 studies (24 in meta-analysis)
items.sample: Children and adolescents, N=1882 in meta-analysis
items.finding: ICBT yielded a moderate between-group effect versus waitlist (g=0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.84) across 11 disorders. Study quality and reporting of variables such as therapist time and adherence varied widely.
items.limitations: Covers many disorders, not depression specifically; youth population; waitlist comparators; variable study quality.

items.method: app store review and content analysis
items.sample: 1054 apps identified, 243 unique depression apps included
items.finding: Of 243 depression apps, about a third mainly provided therapeutic treatment (33.7%) and about a third psychoeducation (32.1%). The abstract describes marketplace content, not clinical efficacy.
items.limitations: Based on app store descriptions only; no efficacy or outcome data.

items.method: systematic review (PRISMA, narrative synthesis, quality assessment)
items.sample: College student samples; number of studies not stated in abstract
items.finding: The review assesses effectiveness, usability, acceptability, uptake, and adoption of digital mental health interventions for depression, anxiety and well-being in college students. The abstract excerpt gives no results.
items.limitations: Narrative synthesis; student population only; abstract truncated so results are not visible.

items.method: systematic review of blended face-to-face and internet interventions
items.sample: 64 publications describing 44 studies, 27 of them randomized
items.finding: The review maps formats, treatment stages, and objectives of blended interventions for depression, anxiety, and substance abuse, and assesses their effectiveness. The abstract excerpt does not report effect results.
items.limitations: Covers several disorders; heterogeneous designs; abstract truncated before results.

items.method: Cochrane systematic review of RCTs
items.sample: Post-stroke patients; sample size not stated in abstract
items.finding: The review evaluates pharmaceutical, psychological, and ECT treatments for post-stroke depression. The abstract excerpt reports no digital intervention and no results.
items.limitations: Not about digital therapeutics; 2008 search; abstract truncated.

items.method: systematic review and meta-regression of 31 RCTs, GRADE
items.sample: Youth with depression, 4335 participants
items.finding: Moderate-quality evidence showed face-to-face CBT reduced depressive symptoms at end of treatment and at follow-up, and CBT as indicated prevention gave 63% less risk of depression at follow-up. Persistence of effects is informative but not for digital delivery.
items.limitations: Not specific to digital delivery; youth only; abstract truncated.

items.method: human-centered design study with interview study (n=15 iCBT supporters)
items.sample: 15 iCBT supporters
items.finding: The paper describes developing an AI tool to predict outcomes for human-supported iCBT for depression and anxiety, informed by supporter interviews. It does not measure symptom reduction or durability.
items.limitations: Design and process paper; no efficacy outcomes; small qualitative sample.

items.method: pragmatic randomized waitlist-controlled trial with cost-effectiveness analysis, 8 weeks, 3-month diagnostic follow-up
items.sample: 361 participants referred to IAPT Step 2 (iCBT 241, waitlist 120)
items.finding: The 8-week iCBT trial in IAPT stepped-care assessed PHQ-9 depressive symptoms against a waitlist, with diagnostic interviews at 3 months. The abstract excerpt does not give effect sizes.
items.limitations: Waitlist control (no attention control); short follow-up; abstract truncated before results.

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: The review covers ketamine and esketamine for depression, noting rapid antidepressant effects lasting three to seven days after a single infusion. It concerns a pharmacological treatment, not digital therapeutics.
items.limitations: Off-topic pharmacological treatment; narrative review without stated method.

items.method: mixed-methods study: single-group before-after quasi-experiment plus interviews
items.sample: 20 older adults with depression in four long-term care facilities in Taiwan
items.finding: Participants had no significant changes during the 8-week observation phase; the abstract excerpt is cut off before the intervention results. The Paro social robot is a technology-based, not a conventional digital therapeutic, intervention.
items.limitations: Small sample, no control group, single-group design; abstract truncated.

items.method: longitudinal observational study n=239
items.sample: 239 patients with confirmed COVID-19 and persistent complaints, recruited from online long COVID peer support groups
items.finding: At 3 months, 46.9% had depressive symptoms (HADS ≥8), with PTSD and anxiety symptoms also common; outcomes were assessed up to 6 months after symptom onset. This is a natural-course study, not a digital intervention.
items.limitations: Not a digital therapeutic study; self-selected peer-support group sample; mostly female; no control group

items.method: pilot pre-post mHealth intervention study with 12-month follow-up
items.sample: 77 people living with HIV at a Ryan White clinic
items.finding: Retention in care rose from 51% at baseline to 88% at 6 months and 81% at 12 months. The abstract does not report depressive symptom outcomes.
items.limitations: Not targeted at depression; single clinic; no control group; pilot design

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (16 comparisons)
items.sample: adults with depression; 14 RCTs
items.finding: Meta-analysis of computerised CBT RCTs with adequate concealment and blinded outcome assessment, evaluating short-term effectiveness, long-term effects, functional improvement and dropout. The abstract is truncated, so the effect sizes are not available.
items.limitations: Self-reported primary outcomes in all trials; abstract truncated

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 RCTs (21 in meta-analyses)
items.sample: 8138 participants in prevention interventions and 5195 cannabis users in treatment interventions
items.finding: Digital interventions reduced cannabis use at post-treatment (prevention g=0.33; treatment g=0.12) compared with controls, and prevention effects were maintained at follow-up. The outcome is cannabis use rather than depression.
items.limitations: Outcome is substance use, not depression; self-reported use; small effect for treatment interventions

items.method: systematic review of 208 articles (qualitative and quantitative)
items.sample: 208 empirical studies on digital mental health interventions
items.finding: Engagement barriers included severe mental health issues, technical issues and a lack of personalization. The review identifies end-user, program-content and technology/implementation factors that influence engagement.
items.limitations: Covers mental health in general rather than depression specifically; heterogeneous methods; does not link engagement to symptom outcomes (per the abstract)

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 RCTs
items.sample: 14 RCTs comparing guided vs. unguided or different guidance formats of internet-based interventions
items.finding: Guided interventions were superior to unguided ones for symptom severity (SMD=-0.27), completed modules (SMD=0.52) and completer rate (OR=2.76).
items.limitations: Few trials per guidance-dose and e-coach qualification comparison; covers mental health conditions broadly rather than depression only

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
items.sample: university students; trials of computer-delivered and web-based interventions for depression, anxiety and stress
items.finding: The review evaluates the effectiveness of web-based and computer-delivered interventions on depression, anxiety and stress in university students. The abstract is truncated, so results are not available.
items.limitations: Student population only; abstract truncated; mixed outcomes beyond depression

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 comparisons
items.sample: n=4226 adults in web- and computer-based stress-management trials
items.finding: Stress interventions had a small effect on depression at posttest (d=0.34) and larger effects on stress for guided than unguided formats (d=0.64 for guided). Follow-up data at 1-3 and 4-6 months were assessed for stress only.
items.limitations: Primary outcome is stress and depression is secondary; follow-up assessed for stress only; population not selected for depression

items.method: systematic review with meta-analysis of 9 RCTs vs. no-intervention control and 6 vs. active control, plus thematic synthesis of 41 studies
items.sample: young people; 15 RCTs in meta-analysis and 41 studies in narrative synthesis
items.finding: Digital interventions had a moderate pooled effect on depression in young people compared with no-intervention control (d=0.33, 95% CI 0.11-0.55). The review also examined factors related to adherence, engagement and outcomes, and compared with active controls.
items.limitations: Young-people population only; mixed-methods synthesis; small number of RCTs; abstract truncated

items.method: RCT n=76 (guided vs unguided vs waitlist)
items.sample: 76 individuals with major depression or dysthymia; 69 (91%) completed posttreatment and 59 (78%) the 6-month follow-up
items.finding: Both guided and unguided internet treatments significantly reduced depressive symptoms compared with waiting-list control, with a BDI-II between-group effect size of d=0.66 for unguided at posttreatment. Follow-up was at 6 months.
items.limitations: Small sample; single trial; waitlist control only; abstract truncated

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (35 studies narrative, 25 meta-analyzed)
items.sample: 35 eligible studies; 25 with sufficient data for meta-analysis
items.finding: Greater engagement with digital mental health interventions was significantly associated with better post-intervention outcomes (correlational r = 0.24; between-groups Hedges' g = 0.40). The association held regardless of intervention type (unguided/guided).
items.limitations: Outcomes are broad mental health, not depression-specific; engagement-outcome link is correlational and may be confounded; abstract is truncated and gives no follow-up data.

items.method: meta-analysis of 16 RCTs (23 comparisons)
items.sample: 5,612 participants with adult alcohol misuse
items.finding: Internet interventions for alcohol misuse had a small but significant overall effect versus controls (g = 0.20), with participants drinking about 22 g less ethanol and more likely to meet low-risk guidelines at post-treatment. The paper compares guided and unguided formats, but the outcome is alcohol use, not depression.
items.limitations: Population and outcome are alcohol misuse, not depression; only post-treatment outcomes are reported in the abstract.

items.method: RCT (two trials, n=235)
items.sample: 235 participants with social anxiety disorder
items.finding: Guided internet-based treatment and unguided bibliotherapy both outperformed waiting list on social anxiety, general anxiety, depression and quality of life. Gains were well maintained at one year.
items.limitations: Population has social anxiety disorder, so depression is a secondary outcome; waiting-list control; unguided arm was bibliotherapy rather than a digital format.

items.method: systematic app identification with functionality analysis and user review analysis
items.finding: The study analyzed the therapeutic functionality and engagement features of CBT apps for depression and user opinions about them, to identify factors affecting user experience and engagement. The abstract is truncated and reports no clinical outcomes.
items.limitations: No symptom outcomes; relies on app store functionality and user reviews; abstract is truncated.

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: The review discusses the lack of a consensus definition of treatment-resistant depression, its estimated prevalence (at least 30% of persons with depression) and management. The abstract does not address digital therapeutics.
items.limitations: Narrative review of treatment-resistant depression; no digital intervention evidence in the abstract.

items.method: systematic review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
items.finding: The review assesses the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of eHealth interventions in somatic diseases, based on reviews published 2009-2012. The abstract gives no depression-specific results.
items.limitations: Somatic disease population, not depression; abstract truncated before results; review of reviews.

items.method: meta-analysis of 29 RCTs
items.sample: 1,628 subjects with social anxiety disorder
items.finding: Psychological treatments for social anxiety disorder had a mean effect size of 0.70 on depression measures (19 contrast groups). Waiting-list controlled studies showed larger effects than placebo or treatment-as-usual controls.
items.limitations: Not digital-specific; depression is a secondary outcome in social anxiety patients; heterogeneity and variable study quality.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 118 RCTs
items.sample: 45,924 school-aged participants
items.finding: School-based prevention programs had small post-intervention effects on depression (g = 0.21) and anxiety (g = 0.18), with larger effects for targeted than universal programs. External providers showed some benefit over school staff.
items.limitations: Prevention programs in schools, not specifically digital therapeutics; the population is youth rather than adults with clinical depression.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of eHealth trials with quality/bias assessment
items.sample: employee populations
items.finding: The review evaluates the effectiveness of app- or web-based mental health interventions for employees, stratified by follow-up length, intervention type, and universal versus targeted delivery. The abstract is truncated, so effect sizes are not available.
items.limitations: Occupational population; mental health outcomes broader than depression; abstract is truncated and gives no results.

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: The review covers the rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine and its synaptic mechanisms. It does not address digital therapeutics.
items.limitations: Pharmacological mechanism review; off-topic for digital interventions.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs
items.sample: 10 RCTs of eHealth prevention interventions for anxiety and depression in the general population
items.finding: Ten RCTs, all using cognitive behavioural techniques and judged of sufficient quality, were pooled with a random-effects model to estimate the effects of eHealth prevention programs. The abstract is truncated before the effect sizes.
items.limitations: Prevention in the general population rather than treatment of clinical depression; only 10 trials; abstract truncated

items.method: two-arm parallel individually randomised controlled trial
items.sample: community sample of mothers with persistent postnatal major depression, infants aged 4.5-9 months at recruitment
items.finding: Tested whether parenting video-feedback therapy versus progressive muscle relaxation, both added to CBT, improves child outcomes at age 2 for persistent postnatal depression. The abstract does not report results.
items.limitations: Face-to-face therapy rather than a digital therapeutic; primary outcomes are child outcomes; abstract truncated

items.method: systematic literature review (PRISMA), 17 studies
items.sample: 17 studies of eHealth in palliative care
items.finding: No RCTs of eHealth in palliative care were found; studies were mostly observational, non-controlled or quasi-experimental and highly heterogeneous.
items.limitations: Palliative care setting, not depression; no RCTs; heterogeneous studies

items.method: narrative review of adequately powered RCTs
items.sample: patients with insomnia and comorbid MDD, GAD or PTSD
items.finding: CBT-I may improve depression and anxiety outcomes in patients with comorbid insomnia and is superior to traditional depression/anxiety treatment for insomnia symptoms. Results are mixed on whether CBT-I alone or augmented has effects on depression outcomes.
items.limitations: Narrative review; not specific to digital delivery; mixed results

items.method: systematic review of 78 studies (62 interventions), narrative synthesis
items.sample: family carers of people with long term illness
items.finding: eHealth interventions for carers were mostly psychoeducational and delivered via an enriched online environment. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, so the findings were synthesised narratively.
items.limitations: Carer population, not depression-focused; no meta-analysis due to heterogeneity

items.method: systematic review of RCTs of internet interventions for anxiety and depression
items.finding: Attrition in RCTs ranged from about 1% to 50%, lower than in open-access sites. Predictors of adherence included disease severity, treatment length and chronicity, but few studies examined reasons for dropout or used appropriate statistical techniques.
items.limitations: Older review (2009); does not link adherence to symptom outcomes; poor statistical handling in primary studies

items.method: systematic review of 19 studies
items.sample: 19 studies of internet-based treatment with minimal therapist contact for psychological disorders
items.finding: Dropout ranged from 2% to 83%, with a weighted average of 31%. Evidence on specific variables predicting dropout was inconclusive.
items.limitations: Covers various psychological disorders, not only depression; two databases; inconclusive predictors

items.method: individual patient data meta-analysis of 10 RCTs
items.sample: 2705 participants in 10 RCTs of self-guided web-based depression interventions
items.finding: Male gender (RR 1.08), lower education (primary, RR 1.26) and comorbid anxiety symptoms (RR 1.18) were among the significant predictors of dropout from self-guided web-based interventions for depression.
items.limitations: Focuses on dropout predictors, not symptom outcomes or persistence; only self-guided interventions; abstract truncated

items.method: survey (narrative review) of sensing and machine-learning research
items.finding: Surveys sensor- and machine-learning-based mental health monitoring systems and proposes a taxonomy, challenges and future opportunities.
items.limitations: About monitoring, not treatment; no effectiveness data; no systematic method described

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: Engagement with digital mental health interventions is influenced by patient-, intervention- and systems-level factors. Human support, gamification, financial incentives and persuasive technology may improve engagement.
items.limitations: No systematic method stated; does not quantify effects on symptom outcomes

items.method: RCT (wait-list controlled)
items.sample: Patients with major depressive episode; n=38 intervention (CBM-I + iCBT) vs n=31 wait-list
items.finding: Intent-to-treat analyses showed significant reductions in depressive symptoms and distress with medium-large effects (Cohen's d = 0.62-2.40) after CBM-I and the combined CBM-I + iCBT intervention versus wait-list. Change in interpretation bias partially mediated the symptom reduction after CBM-I.
items.limitations: Small sample; wait-list control (no attention control); abstract truncated and gives no follow-up data or adherence results

items.method: RCT n=42
items.sample: 42 pregnant women (gestational week 12-28) with major depression; ICBT add-on to usual care vs TAU
items.finding: Tested a pregnancy-adapted 10-week ICBT program as an add-on to usual care against TAU on MADRS-S, with acceptability and adherence also assessed. The abstract excerpt is cut off before the results, so the effect size is not stated.
items.limitations: Small sample; TAU comparator; results not visible in the abstract; self-referred participants

items.method: Single-blind 3-arm RCT n=148
items.sample: 148 Chinese university students with depressive symptoms; chatbot (n=49), e-book (n=49), general chatbot (n=50)
items.finding: Compared a CBT-based chatbot (XiaoE) with an e-book and a general chatbot control for 1 week, with PHQ-9 measured at 1 week and 1 month. Results are not shown in the abstract excerpt.
items.limitations: Very short 1-week intervention; short follow-up of 1 month; young university sample; results truncated in abstract

items.method: narrative review/commentary (unclear from abstract)
items.finding: Argues that digital mental health tools show promising efficacy in trials but face challenges in sustained implementation and evaluation. Notes the limits of traditional research methods for evaluating digital mental health.
items.limitations: No stated methods or quantitative data; not specific to depression outcomes

items.method: real-world data evaluation, mixed-methods study
items.finding: Presents a preliminary real-world evaluation of Wysa, an AI conversational agent for mental well-being, in the context of depression burden. The abstract excerpt does not report outcomes.
items.limitations: Observational real-world app data without controlled comparison; abstract truncated; likely self-selected users

items.method: conceptual review proposing a taxonomy
items.finding: Proposes four categories of Internet-supported therapeutic interventions (web-based interventions, online counseling/therapy, Internet-operated therapeutic software, other online activities). Provides definitions and terminology rather than efficacy data.
items.limitations: No effectiveness data; definitional paper; dated (2009)

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: Reviews evidence that therapist-guided ICBT is more effective than waitlist for depression and anxiety and tends to be as effective as face-to-face CBT. A significant minority experience negative effects, with deterioration rates similar to face-to-face treatment and lower than control conditions.
items.limitations: Narrative review without stated systematic methods; limited focus on long-term persistence; few consistent moderators identified

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 nonrandomized pre-post studies (30 groups)
items.sample: Adults treated for depression or anxiety with guided iCBT in routine care; 19 studies
items.finding: Pre-post effect sizes were clinically relevant (Hedges' g=0.42-1.88; pooled 1.78 for depression), with moderate to high acceptability. Average deterioration was 2.9%.
items.limitations: Nonrandomized pre-post designs without controls; high heterogeneity; pooled effect likely inflated; guided iCBT only

items.method: narrative review/commentary
items.finding: Describes the metaverse and NFTs and their potential application to mental health treatment via VR/AR/MR. States that studies have reported positive results but gives no specific data on depression.
items.limitations: Speculative; no depression-specific outcomes or methods; no quantitative evidence

items.method: expert consensus development panel
items.sample: International cross-disciplinary expert panel
items.finding: The panel proposed a framework for digital mental health research and implementation. Key themes include transdiagnostic approaches and the need for organisational change and extended clinical roles such as digital navigators.
items.limitations: Expert opinion rather than empirical data; not specific to depression efficacy or durability

items.method: unclear from abstract
items.finding: The abstract contains only table-of-contents fragments (quality of life outcomes for acupuncture versus control acupuncture); no findings on digital therapeutics are reported.
items.limitations: Abstract is uninformative; the topic is acupuncture, not digital interventions, so it is off-topic.

items.method: systematic review
items.finding: The abstract states that this review examines online interventions for depression in young people, covering RCTs of intervention content and social-networking-based interventions, in order to identify features linked to treatment outcomes. The abstract is truncated before results, so no effect sizes or conclusions are available.
items.limitations: Abstract is truncated, so the number of studies and the results are not stated. The population is young people only, which is adjacent to the general target population.

items.method: commentary
items.finding: The paper argues that digital mental health can enhance, but not replace, existing services. It describes benefits such as accessibility, a 'poly-digital' aggregation of marginal gains, and real-world data collection through digital phenotyping and ecological momentary assessment.
items.limitations: This is a perspective piece with no empirical data on depressive symptom outcomes or their durability.

items.method: meta-analysis of 12 studies (15 comparisons)
items.sample: 2446 participants; 10 of 12 studies Internet-delivered
items.finding: Internet/computerized treatments outperformed controls at posttest (d = 0.41, 95% CI 0.29-0.54). Supported treatments had a larger effect (d = 0.61) than unsupported ones (d = 0.25).
items.limitations: Small number of studies; authors say more studies are needed; abstract reports posttest effects only, no follow-up durability.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, random-effects model
items.sample: 13 randomized trials, 796 children and adolescents (up to age 25); 4 depression-only trials, 2 transdiagnostic
items.finding: The abstract states the aim of evaluating cCBT for anxiety and depression in youth, but the overall effect size is cut off. Only 4 of the 13 trials targeted depression alone.
items.limitations: Youth population; anxiety and depression pooled; few depression-specific trials; abstract truncated before results.

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: The review reports a strong correlation between degree of clinician support and outcome in internet-delivered CBT for depression. It also covers variation in treatment content and therapist factors.
items.limitations: Narrative review with no stated search method or quantitative synthesis; no follow-up data in abstract.

items.method: meta-analysis of 24 studies (26 treatment conditions)
items.sample: Adults with depression; 14 face-to-face CBT and 12 guided iCBT conditions
items.finding: The abstract describes the comparison of adherence (percentage of completed sessions and completers) between guided iCBT and face-to-face CBT. The results are truncated, and no head-to-head trials met the inclusion criteria.
items.limitations: Indirect comparisons across trials; adherence rather than symptom outcome; community samples without somatic comorbidity or substance abuse; results truncated.

items.method: phase II RCT, n=42
items.sample: 42 adults with medication-refractory residual depression
items.finding: Adding individual rumination-focused CBT to treatment as usual significantly improved residual symptoms and remission rates, with effects mediated by reduced rumination.
items.limitations: Face-to-face therapy, not digital; small sample; no attention control group.

items.method: pragmatic multicentre three-arm RCT (REEACT)
items.sample: Adults in primary care with PHQ-9 ≥ 10
items.finding: Supported cCBT (Beating the Blues or MoodGYM) added to usual GP care gave no additional improvement in depression over usual care alone. Outcomes were assessed at 4, 12 and 24 months.
items.limitations: Allocation not blinded; usual care unconstrained; abstract truncated before the numerical results.

items.method: three-arm RCT
items.sample: Adults with self-reported depression in a nonprofit health maintenance organization; sample size not stated in abstract
items.finding: The trial tested whether reminders (postcard or telephone) would make a pure self-help internet program (ODIN) effective, since earlier unguided trials were negative. The abstract is truncated before the results.
items.limitations: Self-reported depression; results not shown in abstract; older program.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 34 RCTs
items.sample: 3113 children and adolescents aged 6-18 with depression and anxiety
items.finding: Technology-delivered interventions showed a small-to-moderate effect versus waiting list (g = 0.45, 95% CI 0.29-0.60). CBT results are cut off in the abstract.
items.limitations: Youth population; depression and anxiety pooled; mostly waitlist comparators; heterogeneous intervention types.

items.method: RCT, n=299
items.sample: 299 depressed adults in a health maintenance organization (144 intervention, 155 no-access control); mean intake scores in the severe range
items.finding: The trial evaluated the ODIN web-based cognitive therapy self-help program against no access, with CES-D assessed at 4, 8, 16 and 32 weeks. The abstract is truncated before the outcome results.
items.limitations: Unguided and standalone; control group could use usual care; results not shown in abstract; older program.

items.method: three-arm RCT, n=946
items.sample: 946 patients with mild to moderate depression recruited in Swedish primary healthcare centres
items.finding: Both exercise and internet-based CBT produced larger improvements in depressive symptoms than treatment as usual at the 3-month reassessment. Work capacity improved in all three groups with no significant differences.
items.limitations: Only a short follow-up (3 months, 78% response rate); unblinded behavioural trial; no long-term persistence data in abstract.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Cochrane RoB 2.0 quality assessment)
items.sample: adolescents and young adults aged 12-25 with anxiety or depressive symptoms; number of trials not stated in the abstract excerpt
items.finding: The review examines posttreatment and follow-up effects of computerized CBT versus active and passive controls, and explores moderators of effect. Effect sizes are not given in the available abstract text.
items.limitations: Abstract is truncated, so results are not visible; restricted to youth, so generalizability to adults is limited.

items.method: RCT n=155, four arms
items.sample: 155 callers to a national helpline with moderate to high psychological distress
items.finding: Web-based CBT, with or without telephone tracking, produced lower depression than treatment as usual at post-intervention and at 6-month follow-up. Lay telephone tracking added no benefit for symptoms or adherence.
items.limitations: Modest sample, single helpline setting, follow-up limited to 6 months, comparison with treatment as usual rather than attention control.

items.method: network meta-analysis of 101 RCTs
items.sample: 11,910 adult patients with depression, mostly moderate to severe
items.finding: Combined psychotherapy plus pharmacotherapy was more effective than either alone (RR=1.27 vs psychotherapy; RR=1.25 vs pharmacotherapy) for treatment response. Chronic/treatment-resistant depression and baseline severity were assessed as moderators.
items.limitations: Not about digital interventions; relevance is limited to adjunct versus standalone and moderator context.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, random-effects model
items.sample: 19 trials, 3681 adults with heightened symptom severity; depression k=6
items.finding: Standalone smartphone apps showed a small-to-moderate effect on depression (Hedges' g = 0.33, 95% CI 0.10-0.57) versus control. Evidence for other mental health outcomes was mixed or presented narratively.
items.limitations: Few depression trials (k=6); search dates to February 2018; follow-up durability not evident from the abstract.

items.method: individual patient data meta-analysis of 16 datasets
items.sample: 2470 patients with depression in primary care and community settings
items.finding: There was a significant interaction between baseline severity and treatment effect: more severely depressed patients showed larger benefits from low intensity interventions (guided self-help, internet-delivered) versus usual care. The abstract is truncated before the magnitude of the effect is given.
items.limitations: Low intensity interventions are broader than digital-only; abstract truncated; effect-size interaction is small.

items.method: blinded randomized split-plot trial n=107
items.sample: 107 adults with major depressive disorder and insomnia (mean age 42)
items.finding: All groups improved on subjective sleep efficiency and total wake time with large effects, with no significant group differences. CBT-I groups improved on objective total wake time while the antidepressant plus sleep hygiene group worsened.
items.limitations: Therapist-delivered 4-session CBT-I rather than digital; primary outcomes are sleep rather than depression; modest sample, two sites.

items.method: semi-structured expert interviews n=5
items.sample: 5 therapists in the German arm of the E-Compared RCT of blended therapy for depression (N=173 patients)
items.finding: The study identified therapist-perceived barriers and facilitators to implementing blended therapy (face-to-face plus internet/mobile CBT) for depression, using the theoretical domains framework. Specific findings are not visible in the truncated abstract.
items.limitations: Very small qualitative pilot, therapist perspective only, no clinical outcomes.

items.method: individual participant data meta-analysis of 13 RCTs
items.sample: 3805 adults with depressive symptoms receiving self-guided iCBT or control
items.finding: Clinically significant deterioration occurred in 7.2% of participants overall, with lower rates in the self-guided iCBT group (5.8%) than in controls (9.1%). Socio-demographic, clinical and study-level moderators of deterioration were tested.
items.limitations: Only 13 of 16 eligible trials provided data; focuses on deterioration rather than overall efficacy or durability.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA), random-effects
items.sample: clinical trials of CBT-I with quality-of-life outcomes; number not stated in the abstract excerpt
items.finding: The review synthesizes CBT-I effects on quality of life across populations, delivery modes and methods. Results are not shown in the truncated abstract.
items.limitations: Outcome is quality of life in insomnia, not depressive symptoms; abstract truncated.

items.method: individual patient data meta-analysis of 18 RCTs (21 comparisons)
items.sample: 2079 adults with depression in Internet-based guided self-help trials
items.finding: Reliable deterioration from baseline to post-treatment was less likely with the intervention than control (3.36% vs 7.60%; RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.29-0.75). Lower education was associated with higher deterioration risk.
items.limitations: Covers deterioration to post-treatment only; guided self-help only; abstract truncated.

items.method: systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of RCTs
items.sample: people with knee and/or hip osteoarthritis
items.finding: The abstract describes an IPD meta-analysis of patient-level moderators of therapeutic exercise effects on pain and physical function in osteoarthritis at 12 weeks, 6 months and 12 months. It does not address depression or digital therapeutics.
items.limitations: Off-topic population and intervention; abstract truncated before results.

items.method: individual participant data meta-analysis of 7 RCTs
items.sample: 7 trials, 2,186 adults with subthreshold depression
items.finding: Internet-based interventions were superior to controls on depressive symptom severity at posttreatment (g=0.39), 3-6 month follow-up (g=0.30) and 12-month follow-up (g=0.27). Response and close to symptom-free status were also more frequent in the intervention group at all time points.
items.limitations: Subthreshold depression only, with few trials; the abstract is truncated before the moderator and deterioration results.

items.method: systematic literature review of 94 studies (756 unique records screened)
items.sample: 94 clinical, feasibility and pilot studies of digital interventions in adults with depression/MDD
items.finding: The review assessed how adherence and engagement with digital depression interventions are measured and reported, and whether higher adherence or engagement is linked to greater efficacy. The abstract is truncated before the results.
items.limitations: Results are not visible in the abstract; the included studies are heterogeneous, including pilot and feasibility studies.

items.method: systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 RCTs
items.sample: 22 RCTs of adults with insomnia reporting depressive or anxiety symptoms
items.finding: At post-treatment, digital CBT-I had a small to moderate effect on depressive symptoms (SMD=-0.42, k=21) and on anxiety (SMD=-0.29), and a large effect on sleep (SMD=-0.76). Higher-adherence groups showed larger effects on depression, anxiety and sleep than lower-adherence groups.
items.limitations: Population is people with insomnia, not primarily depression, and depression is a secondary outcome; the abstract is truncated, so follow-up persistence is not shown.

consensus.statement: In adults with depression, internet CBT beat mostly waitlist, usual-care or no-access controls at post-treatment, with small-to-moderate effects (d=0.41; g=0.39 in subthreshold depression; d=0.66 for unguided CBT vs waitlist in one small trial; superior to TAU at 3 months in primary care). Standalone apps show g=0.33 (k=6), and a transdiagnostic app meta-analysis gives g=0.28 that stayed robust after adjusting for control type and risk of bias, but that one is indirect for clinical depression.

Effects in youth (d=0.33 vs no intervention; g=0.45 for pooled depression and anxiety vs mostly waitlist) are similar in size. Estimates from the 2006 mixed anxiety/depression meta-analysis (d=0.27-0.32), the stress-management review (d=0.34, depression secondary) and the insomnia review (SMD=-0.42) are indirect for clinical depression.

Gains persisted at follow-up in the studies with numerical data: g=0.30 at 3-6 months and g=0.27 at 12 months in subthreshold depression, and lower depression than TAU at 6 months in helpline callers. This is a modest shrinkage, not a loss, but the numbers come mainly from one IPD analysis of subthreshold depression and one modest-sized trial.

Reliable deterioration was less frequent with internet interventions than with control conditions in IPD meta-analyses (3.4% vs 7.6%; 5.8% vs 9.1%). A narrative review agrees, and an uncontrolled pre-post synthesis reports 2.9% deterioration, which is not comparable because it has no control.

Supported or guided formats tend to outperform unguided ones. Evidence comes from broad mental-health meta-analyses (SMD=-0.27 for symptom severity; d=0.61 vs 0.25), not depression-specific direct comparisons. Low-reliability narrative reviews support clinician support only as an engagement mechanism, and the stress guided advantage (d=0.64) is excluded as evidence for depression severity.

Higher engagement or adherence is associated with larger benefit (r=0.24; g=0.40 in broad mental health; larger depression effects in higher-adherence insomnia groups), but the link is correlational. Attrition is substantial (weighted mean dropout 31%, up to 50-83%).

conflicts.claim: Whether digital CBT adds benefit in primary care (a design and context discrepancy, not a direct disagreement).

side_a.statement: Supported cCBT added to usual GP care gave no additional improvement over usual care at 4, 12 and 24 months.

side_b.statement: Internet CBT beat treatment as usual in primary care at 3 months and in helpline callers at 6 months.

conflicts.hypothesis_for_conflict: REEACT tested add-on use against unconstrained usual care in unblinded patients with PHQ-9 of 10 or more, while the others used standalone iCBT against TAU, with different programs, support and follow-up lengths. Any benefit may have been diluted by active usual care or low uptake.

conflicts.claim: Whether added human contact improves outcomes (a scope discrepancy).

side_a.statement: Lay telephone tracking added no benefit for symptoms or adherence.

side_b.statement: Guided interventions outperformed unguided ones for symptom severity and completion across mental-health conditions.

conflicts.hypothesis_for_conflict: Lay telephone tracking is a minimal form of support compared with the clinician or e-coach guidance in the pooled trials. The single helpline trial is small and the review is not depression-specific.

conditional.statement: Baseline severity moderates benefit: more severely depressed patients gained more from low-intensity interventions (guided self-help, internet) than from usual care. The effect interaction is small and the category is broader than digital-only.
Lower education raised deterioration risk, and male sex, lower education and comorbid anxiety predicted dropout from self-guided web interventions.

Very large pre-post effects (pooled g=1.78 for depression) hold only as uncontrolled estimates for guided iCBT in routine care and are likely inflated, so they should not be compared with RCT effects.

synthesis.coverage_note: The evidence is strong for short-term effects (rq1), with mostly small-to-moderate effects against waitlist or TAU controls, and for deterioration (rq6) from IPD meta-analyses. Durability (rq2) has numerical estimates only to 12 months in subthreshold depression. Results from the IPD network meta-analysis (6- and 12-month guided vs unguided) and the 2013 meta-analysis were not retrieved because of truncated abstracts, so that is a retrieval gap, with residual gaps beyond 12 months and in attention-controlled comparisons. Moderators (rq4), guidance effects specific to depression (rq3) and placebo or attention-control effects (rq6) are thin, with truncated results and population-specific or indirect reviews. Missing are IPD or meta-regression moderator results for comorbidity, setting and adjunct vs standalone use, long-term follow-up RCTs, and sham or attention-controlled trials.

gaps.description: Numerical durability estimates for clinical depression stop at 12 months, and even those come from subthreshold samples (g=0.27). The 6- and 12-month guided vs unguided estimates in the IPD network meta-analysis and the long-term results of the 2013 meta-analysis were not retrieved, so their numbers are unknown to us. Residual gaps are follow-up beyond 12 months, relapse timing, and how to keep a comparison once waitlist controls are treated.
gaps.proposed_rq: In adults with diagnosed major depression, how much of the post-treatment reduction in PHQ-9 from internet CBT remains at 12, 24 and 36 months, and when do relapses occur?
gaps.method: First extract the 6- and 12-month estimates from the existing IPD and meta-analyses, then run a pre-registered IPD meta-analysis of trials with at least 12-month follow-up, modelling PHQ-9 trajectories and time to relapse. Add a 24-36 month registry-linked follow-up of a completed iCBT trial cohort.
gaps.data: IPD from the iCBT depression trials in the existing IPD consortia (13-42 trials) plus original trial authors' long-term data. Cohort follow-up could use IAPT or primary-care records and outcome questionnaires.

gaps.description: Most depression effects come from waitlist, TAU or no-access controls, and the placebo or attention component is unquantified. The only sham-like comparison is a 1-week chatbot trial with truncated results, and the transdiagnostic app estimate is not specific to clinical depression. Small waitlist trials may overstate specific effects.
gaps.proposed_rq: How much of the effect of digital depression treatment over waitlist remains when it is compared with an attention-control or sham digital condition in clinically depressed adults?
gaps.method: Meta-regression of control type (waitlist, TAU, attention or sham) on depression effect sizes, restricted to clinical depression, plus a pre-registered three-arm RCT (iCBT vs attention-control app vs waitlist, 8-12 weeks). The primary outcome is PHQ-9 at post-treatment and at 6 months, with the attention-control arm offered iCBT after follow-up.
gaps.data: Existing trial registries and the meta-analytic databases for coding control type. The RCT needs about 300 adults with PHQ-9 of 10 or more, recruited from primary care or online.

gaps.description: Moderators of symptom outcome are essentially untested in the retrieved results. Baseline severity shows only a small interaction with a broad 'low-intensity' category, while the REEACT trial found no add-on benefit and the Swedish trial found benefit over TAU, leaving adjunct vs standalone use, setting and comorbid anxiety unresolved. The two IPD meta-analyses' moderator results were not visible.
gaps.proposed_rq: Do baseline severity, comorbid anxiety, clinical setting and use as adjunct vs standalone treatment moderate the effect of digital CBT on depressive symptoms?
gaps.method: Two-stage IPD meta-analysis with pre-specified treatment-by-moderator interaction terms on post-treatment PHQ-9, complemented by a pragmatic RCT in primary care randomising adjunct to usual care vs standalone iCBT vs usual care. Compare outcomes at 3 and 12 months.
gaps.data: IPD from the consortia behind the JAMA Psychiatry and BMJ IPD analyses, with harmonised baseline variables. The RCT needs about 450 primary-care patients with PHQ-9 of 10 or more across several practices.

gaps.description: The advantage of guided over unguided formats comes from broad mental-health meta-analyses, not from depression-specific head-to-head comparisons. The only minimal-support test, lay telephone tracking, was small and found nothing. Whether the guidance advantage lasts beyond 12 months or can be replaced by cheaper support is unclear.
gaps.proposed_rq: Among adults with depression, does clinician-guided iCBT produce larger and longer-lasting PHQ-9 reductions than iCBT with automated or lay support, and by how much?
gaps.method: Three-arm non-inferiority RCT comparing clinician-guided, automated-feedback/lay-supported and unguided iCBT, with PHQ-9 at post-treatment, 12 and 24 months. Secondary outcomes are module completion and cost per remission.
gaps.data: About 600 adults with major depression recruited through online screening or IAPT-type services, with pre-specified non-inferiority margin and sample-size calculations.

gaps.description: Deterioration is quantified only from baseline to post-treatment, and engagement is linked to benefit only correlationally. Lower education predicts both deterioration and dropout, but no study has followed deterioration after treatment ends or tested whether adapting to low-education users changes it. The causal role of engagement therefore remains untested.
gaps.proposed_rq: Does an engagement-adaptive version of iCBT reduce deterioration and dropout among lower-education adults compared with standard iCBT, including during 12 months of follow-up?
gaps.method: Two-arm RCT with an adaptive version (simplified content, scheduled prompts) vs standard iCBT, stratified by education. The primary outcome is reliable deterioration on PHQ-9 at post-treatment and 12 months, with engagement mediation analysis.
gaps.data: About 500 adults with depressive symptoms, oversampling those with primary or secondary education only. Recruit through primary care and community outreach.

limitations: Only abstracts and metadata were read, with no full texts; several key results (the IPD network meta-analysis 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2020.4364 with 6- and 12-month guided vs unguided estimates, the 2013 meta-analysis, the moderator results of the two IPD analyses, and the adherence review 10.2196/43727) were truncated, so these gaps are partly retrieval failures rather than true research gaps.

Persistence evidence (g=0.30 at 3-6 months, g=0.27 at 12 months) comes from subthreshold depression and distressed helpline callers, not diagnosed major depression; REEACT's null result at 12 and 24 months argues against generalizing, and no numerical follow-up beyond 12 months was found.

Most effect estimates are against waitlist, TAU or no-access controls, so placebo and attention effects are unquantified; small waitlist trials (e.g., d=0.66 for unguided CBT) may overstate effects, and this unguided estimate is far larger than the pooled unguided estimate.

Guidance, engagement and intervention-type evidence is indirect: guided vs unguided contrasts come from cross-trial comparisons in broad mental-health or non-depression reviews (stress, insomnia, transdiagnostic apps), engagement–outcome links are correlational, and effects are not comparable across web iCBT, apps, chatbots and blended formats.

Moderator and deterioration findings are thin: the baseline-severity interaction is small and uses a broader 'low-intensity' category, severity may raise benefit but lower engagement, deterioration is measured only from baseline to post-treatment, and the very large pre-post effect (g=1.78) is uncontrolled and likely inflated.
The search covered only OpenAlex and arXiv, so relevant trials in other databases may be missed; narrative reviews and commentaries of lower reliability were used only for supporting mechanisms.

executive_summary: 402편의 후보 중 87편을 평가했으며, 주로 인터넷 CBT와 앱에 대한 메타분석, IPD 메타분석, 일부 RCT와 서술적 리뷰로 구성된다. 성인 우울증에서 인터넷 CBT는 주로 대기자·통상치료·무접근 대조군보다 치료 직후 작거나 중간 정도의 효과를 보였고(d=0.41, 준임상 우울 g=0.39), 단독 앱은 g=0.33(k=6)이었으며 청소년도 비슷한 크기(d=0.33)였다. 개선은 추적 시점에도 완만하게 줄어들 뿐 사라지지 않았으나(3-6개월 g=0.30, 12개월 g=0.27), 이 수치는 거의 준임상 우울 IPD 분석과 소규모 시험에서만 나와 진단된 우울증의 지속성은 사실상 확인되지 않았다. 1차 진료에서는 REEACT가 추가 이점을 찾지 못한 반면 스웨덴 시험은 통상치료 대비 이점을 보였는데, 이는 설계와 맥락의 차이이지 직접적 불일치는 아니다. 악화(deterioration)는 대조군보다 인터넷 중재에서 드물었지만(3.4% vs 7.6%), 치료 종료 후 악화 추적은 검색된 근거에서 찾지 못했다. 지도형이 비지도형보다 낫다는 근거는 우울증 특이적 직접 비교가 아닌 광범위한 정신건강 메타분석에 의존하며, 순응도와 효과의 연관성도 상관적이고 중도탈락이 크다(평균 31%). 핵심 공백은 12개월 이후의 지속성과 재발 시점, 주의 통제·가짜 대조 대비 특이 효과, 그리고 보조 vs 단독 사용·동반 불안 같은 조절변수이며, 일부 IPD 결과는 초록이 잘려 확인하지 못한 검색 한계이기도 하다.
